nameStory: The Red-footed Falcon gets its name from its striking bright red or orange-red legs and feet, which stand out dramatically against its darker plumage. This colorful feature makes it unmistakable among falcons, like wearing bright red boots that catch your eye from a distance.
description: The Red-footed Falcon is a small, sleek bird of prey that's extremely rare in New England, with only two recorded sightings ever. Males are slate-gray with rusty-red undertail coverts, while females are more colorful with orange-buff heads and underparts marked with dark streaks. These compact falcons are about the size of an American Kestrel, with pointed wings and the characteristic falcon silhouette built for swift, agile flight.

idTips.label: Bright red legs and feet
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature - vivid orange-red to bright red legs and feet that seem almost glowing, especially visible when perched

idTips.label: Male coloration
idTips.description: Adult males appear dark slate-gray overall with rusty-red undertail coverts and vent area, creating a striking two-toned appearance

idTips.label: Female markings
idTips.description: Females show warm orange-buff on the head and underparts with neat dark streaking, quite different from the plain gray males

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with quick, snappy wingbeats interspersed with brief glides, often hovering like a kestrel when hunting insects

habitat: In New England, this species is an extremely rare vagrant that could potentially appear anywhere during migration, though the only confirmed sighting was on Martha's Vineyard. In its native range, it prefers open grasslands, agricultural areas, and woodland edges where it can hunt insects in flight.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to be seen, but any sighting would most likely occur during peak migration in late April through May.
seasonality.summer: The Martha's Vineyard sighting occurred in August 2004, making late summer the most probable time for vagrant appearances.
seasonality.fall: Possible during migration from August through September, when birds might be blown off course from their European migration routes.
seasonality.winter: Not expected, as these falcons winter in Africa and would not survive New England winters.

funFact: The Red-footed Falcon made ornithological history in 2004 when one appeared on Martha's Vineyard - the very first time this European and Asian species had ever been recorded anywhere in North America, making any New England birder who spots one a witness to something extraordinarily rare!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with an American Kestrel due to similar size, but the Red-footed Falcon's bright red legs are much more vivid than a kestrel's orange-yellow legs. Remember: if the legs look like they're wearing red socks, you've found something very special!
contextualKnowledge: This species represents one of the ultimate 'mega-rarities' in North American birding - a bird so far from its normal range that seeing one is essentially a once-in-a-lifetime event. Any potential sighting should be photographed and reported immediately to local birding authorities for verification.
compareHints: Unlike American Kestrels which show rusty-red backs and tails, Red-footed Falcons are much grayer overall with those distinctive bright red legs. Compared to Merlins, Red-footed Falcons are less heavily marked below and lack the Merlin's bold facial pattern, plus Merlins have yellow (not red) legs.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's falcons, American kestrels are by far the smallest and most colorful, with that distinctive rufous back that neither Merlins nor Peregrine Falcons possess.
Compared to American Kestrels, merlins are stockier with less colorful plumage and never hover while hunting.
Peregrine Falcons are much larger than American Kestrels (which are robin-sized with rusty coloring) and Merlins (which are jay-sized and heavily streaked).

Compared to its falcon relatives in New England, the gyrfalcon dwarfs the robin-sized American kestrel and pigeon-sized merlin, while being noticeably bulkier and broader-winged than the peregrine falcon.
Among New England's falcons, prairie falcons are most similar to peregrine falcons in size and hunting style, but are much paler with sandy-brown tones instead of blue-gray.
